pfas_status.summary: Federal PFOA and PFOS limits are 4 ppt each. Utilities must comply by April 2029; EPA proposed in May 2026 to move that to April 2031 and to drop the limits for PFHxS, PFNA, GenX and the PFAS mixture rule (not final as of June 2026). Connecticut DPH action levels: PFOS 10, PFNA 12, PFOA 16, GenX 19, PFHxS 49, PFHxA 240, PFBS 760, PFBA 1,800 ppt.

utilities.name: Metropolitan District (MDC)
utilities.source_type: EWG Tap Water Database (state-reported test data, 2021–2023; utility's 2025 report could not be retrieved)
utilities.water_source: Reservoirs (Barkhamsted and Nepaug systems, treated in West Hartford area)
notes: MDC says it met all state and federal standards in 2025 (about 400,000 people, 46.7 million gallons/day).
MDC reports none of the 29 PFAS compounds in EPA's 2023 testing were detected, and the six PFAS in the 2024 federal rule were not detected.
Values below are multi-year averages from state data as compiled by EWG, not MDC's 2025 report (the PDF could not be retrieved from here).

utilities.name: Connecticut Water – Northern Western System
utilities.source_type: 2025 annual water quality report (Consumer Confidence Report)
utilities.water_source: Shenipsit Lake plus six well fields (Hunt, Powder Hollow, Spring Lots, Pine Knob, West Suffield, Vernon)
notes: Lead: 90th percentile 2 ppb (below the 15 ppb action level), but 3 of 170 home samples were above the action level; highest single sample 156 ppb.
TTHM: one sample reached 82.6 ppb; compliance is judged on the running annual average (61.0 ppb), which is under the 80 ppb limit.
Radon in source water up to 1,754 pCi/L (no federal standard).
Lead service line inventory completed in 2024: ctwater.com/serviceline.

tthm.name: Total trihalomethanes (TTHM)
tthm.what_it_is: Formed when chlorine reacts with natural organic matter in reservoir water.
tthm.health: EPA: years of drinking water above the limit may cause liver, kidney or nervous system problems and raise cancer risk.

haa5.name: Haloacetic acids (HAA5)
haa5.what_it_is: Another family of chlorine disinfection byproducts.
haa5.health: EPA: years of drinking water above the limit may raise cancer risk.

lead.name: Lead
lead.limit_label: Federal action level (90th percentile of homes; drops to 10 ppb Nov 2027)
lead.what_it_is: Comes mostly from lead service lines, solder and older faucets inside homes, not from the treatment plant.
lead.health: EPA: can cause developmental delays and learning problems in children, and kidney problems and high blood pressure in adults. EPA's health goal for lead is zero.

copper.name: Copper
copper.health: EPA: short-term stomach upset; long-term exposure above the action level may cause liver or kidney damage.

nitrate.name: Nitrate
nitrate.what_it_is: Fertilizer runoff, septic systems and natural deposits.
nitrate.health: EPA: infants under six months who drink water above the limit can become seriously ill ("blue baby" syndrome).

fluoride.name: Fluoride
fluoride.what_it_is: Mostly added at the treatment plant for dental health (target about 0.7 ppm).
fluoride.health: EPA: long-term exposure above 4 ppm can cause bone disease; children can get mottled teeth.

arsenic.name: Arsenic
arsenic.what_it_is: Dissolves into groundwater from certain Connecticut bedrock.
arsenic.health: EPA: long-term exposure above the limit can cause skin damage and circulatory problems and may raise cancer risk.

uranium.name: Uranium
uranium.what_it_is: Naturally present in some Connecticut granites and gneisses.
uranium.health: EPA: long-term exposure above the limit raises cancer risk and can harm the kidneys.

radium.name: Radium 226 + 228
radium.health: EPA: long-term exposure above the limit raises cancer risk.

radon.name: Radon
radon.what_it_is: Radioactive gas from bedrock that dissolves in groundwater and escapes into the air during showers and laundry.
radon.health: CT DPH: radon released from water into indoor air raises lung cancer risk; drinking it raises stomach cancer risk. CT recommends action at 5,000 pCi/L.

barium.name: Barium
barium.health: EPA: long-term exposure above the limit may increase blood pressure.

cadmium.name: Cadmium
cadmium.what_it_is: Corrosion of galvanized pipes and natural deposits.

manganese.name: Manganese
manganese.what_it_is: Natural mineral common in Connecticut groundwater; causes black staining and metallic taste.

sodium.name: Sodium
sodium.limit_label: No federal limit; CT notification level
sodium.what_it_is: Natural salts, road salt runoff and some treatment chemicals.
sodium.health: Relevant mainly for people on a low-sodium diet; talk to your doctor.

pfoa.name: PFOA
pfoa.what_it_is: Industrial chemical that doesn't break down; from manufacturing, firefighting foam and consumer products.
pfoa.health: EPA: linked to liver, immune and heart effects, developmental effects in infants and children, and higher risk of kidney and testicular cancer.

pfos.name: PFOS
pfos.what_it_is: Industrial chemical that doesn't break down; from manufacturing, firefighting foam and consumer products.
pfos.health: EPA: linked to liver, immune and heart effects, developmental effects, and higher risk of liver cancer.

pfhxs.name: PFHxS
pfhxs.limit_label: Federal limit set 2024; EPA proposed removing it (May 2026)
pfhxs.health: EPA: linked to immune, thyroid and liver effects and developmental effects.

pfna.name: PFNA
pfna.limit_label: Federal limit set 2024; EPA proposed removing it (May 2026)
pfna.health: EPA: linked to higher cholesterol, immune and liver effects and developmental effects.

pfbs.name: PFBS
pfbs.limit_label: Part of federal mixture rule (proposed for removal)

private_wells.headline: About 23% of Connecticut residents rely on private wells, which no utility tests.

findings.what: Arsenic above the 10 ppb federal limit
findings.detail: Spatially weighted estimate from more than 2,000 private bedrock wells sampled 2013–2018.

findings.what: Uranium above the 30 ppb federal limit
findings.detail: Same study. Uranium of at least 1 ppb is present across about 45% of the state.

findings.what: Arsenic or uranium above a federal limit
findings.detail: 674 private wells sampled 2013–2015. Highest arsenic 470 ppb (a well in Oxford); highest uranium 766 ppb (a well in Brookfield). Levels vary widely even between neighboring wells.
findings.source: Flanagan & Brown (2017), USGS Open-File Report 2017–1046, with CT DPH

findings.detail: CT DPH recommends every well owner test for radon in both water and air.
findings.source: CT DPH, Radon in Your Well Water (2021)

private_wells.advice: CT DPH advises private well owners to test at least once for arsenic and uranium — they are not part of routine well tests, so you have to ask for them.

method: Largest public water systems in each Connecticut county; 2025 annual water quality reports where retrievable, otherwise EWG Tap Water Database averages of state-reported data (marked).
'Highest location's annual average' is the number federal compliance is judged on for disinfection byproducts.
Lead and copper are judged on the 90th percentile of home tap samples; individual homes can be higher.
A utility listing a town does not mean every home in that town is on that utility.
